params.why: keeps the numerator of the hyperbola small

stem: Determine the $x$-intercept of the hyperbola $y = \frac{{=a}}{x} {=sg} {=abs(q)}$. Give your answer as a coordinate pair $(x, y)$.
solution: At the $x$-intercept the graph meets the $x$-axis, so $y = 0$. Substitute: $0 = \frac{{=a}}{x} {=sg} {=abs(q)}$.
Move the constant term to the other side: $\frac{{=a}}{x} = {=-q}$.
Multiply both sides by $x$ (we know $x \neq 0$ because $x = 0$ is the vertical asymptote): ${=a} = ({=-q}) \cdot x$.
The $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$. There is no $y$-intercept, because $x = 0$ is an asymptote.
notes: Standard tier: the intercept step of the book's three-part method (sign of a, intercepts, asymptotes) for y = a/x + q. The x-intercept is built to be a whole number: x0 and q are drawn and a = -q*x0, with |a| <= 12 so no instance has a large numerator. a is never 0 and q is never 0, so the graph is always a genuine hyperbola with exactly one x-intercept. The marker answer is a plain coordinate pair; every instance has an integer x-coordinate so no LaTeX fraction can enter the marker. The book's own question (ex6-8-57b) only asks for an asymptote, so this family extends the same y = a/x + q skeleton to the intercept step that the objective names.
